S-IV.
COMPARISON BETWEEN DISCRETE AND CONTINUOUS-TIME DYNAMICAL SYSTEMS
We compare the training of multilayered NNs and continuous-time dynamical systems based on the adjoint method.
In the discrete-time dynamical system, the adjoint vector pn is computed recurrently from pn+1 through the adjoint
equation (S13). In contrast, in the continuous-time dynamical system, the adjoint vector p(t) is a function that evolves
according to the adjoint equation (S33). The two adjoint equations have different forms because the system is either
discrete or continuous in time.

In the discrete-time case, the adjoint equation can be written as pn = pn+1F n − pn+1 r n, which is analogous to
the adjoint equation for the backpropagation algorithm (Eq. (S13)). In the continuous-time case, the adjoint equation
(S33) is a differential equation for p(t).

When considering the system from a control perspective, the control signal u(t) is optimized by the continuous-time
dynamical system. The adjoint vector p(t) represents the costate that corresponds to the Lagrange multiplier in the
optimal control problem. The adjoint equation (S33) is the adjoint equation for the optimal control of the dynamical
system, derived from Pontryagin's maximum principle.

In the discrete-time scenario, the adjoint vector pn serves as the Lagrange multiplier for the constraint given by
Eq. (S10). The adjoint equation (S13) is derived by incorporating the discrete-time constraint into the augmented
loss function.

The key difference between the discrete and continuous adjoint equations lies in the form of the adjoint equation itself.
In the discrete case, the adjoint equation is a recurrence relation (Eq. S13), whereas in the continuous case, it is a
